one_paragraph_summary: Correcting local media inaccuracies on the ICC preliminary examination, Panganiban notes that Secretary Roque -- the only Filipino ICC defense counsel -- and ICC Judge Dr. Raul Pangalangan (Roque's former UP law professor) have singular credentials on the ICC. Under the Rome Statute, the ICC's Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) may initiate a preliminary examination only on the request of a member-state, the UN Security Council, or motu proprio -- and Chief Prosecutor Bensouda's initiative was clearly motu proprio, not triggered by Jude Sabio's 77-page complaint against Duterte and 11 officials (in Bensouda's own words, based on 'a number of communications and reports'). A preliminary examination is merely a process of examining information to determine whether there is a reasonable basis to proceed further -- affidavits are 'inputs,' not 'complaints'; the OTP is proactive, unlike the Philippines' passive prosecutors. Before the OTP can proceed to a formal preliminary investigation, it must secure approval from the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber under Article 15 -- a process that can take years (the Afghanistan preliminary examination began in 2007 but the PTC approval was only sought in 2017). The ICC is a judicial entity observing strict 'becoming conduct' -- judges, prosecutors, and lawyers do not socialize except in the courtroom, reminiscent of 1950s-60s Philippine formality. Most crucially, complementarity is the Rome Statute's cornerstone (Article 17): the ICC will decline a case if the state is genuinely willing and able to investigate or prosecute -- so if the Philippines demonstrates genuine domestic action, the ICC will not have jurisdiction.
